source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory
finding: Memory distilled from successes and failures beat no memory, and beat raw-trajectory memory (Synapse) and workflow memory (AWM), on WebArena. Gains held on three backbones.
numbers: WebArena overall SR (684 tasks, pass@1). Gemini-2.5-flash: no memory 40.5, Synapse 42.1, AWM 44.1, ReasoningBank 48.8. Gemini-2.5-pro: 46.7 / 47.7 / 47.6 / 53.9. Claude-3.7-sonnet: 41.7 / 42.6 / 40.8 / 46.3. Steps fell 9.7 to 8.3 (flash).
limits: Gain over no memory is 4.6 to 8.3 points; raw-trajectory Synapse adds only 0.9 to 1.6. Multi subset has 29 tasks. Authors say they did not compare episodic or hierarchical memory forms. Success labels come from an LLM judge.
agent_relevance: Raw stored episodes (Synapse) give small gains; distilled lessons give several times more. Matters for gap 5: for web agents, distilled wins over raw.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory
finding: Failed trajectories help only when they are distilled into lessons. Baselines that store failures raw gain nothing or get worse.
numbers: WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash. Success-only vs with failures: Synapse 40.6 to 41.7, AWM 44.4 to 42.2, ReasoningBank 46.5 to 49.7.
limits: One backbone, one subset, N=187 tasks. Not tested at matched tokens for the failure arm.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 2 for web agents: failures help if turned into contrastive lessons; raw failures are noise.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory
finding: Memory cost and number of retrieved items. ReasoningBank added about 4.3 percent tokens over no memory. Retrieving more experiences lowered success.
numbers: Total tokens per task: no memory 50,847; Synapse 58,515 (+15.1%); AWM 59,373 (+16.8%); ReasoningBank 53,055 (+4.3%), for +20.5% relative success. Experiences retrieved: success 46.0 with 2, 45.5 with 3, 44.4 with 4 (best near 1).
limits: Token rows were reconstructed from garbled PDF text: AWM and ReasoningBank row alignment checked by summing the columns. Which backbone and subset the k-sweep used is not fully clear.
agent_relevance: At roughly equal tokens, distilled beats raw. Supports small k (1) for our agent. Authors: relevance and quality matter more than quantity.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: An Empirical Study of Experience-Following Behavior
finding: Writing every executed case back to memory (add-all) was worse than a frozen small expert-verified memory on all four agents. Only strict (oracle-checked) addition beat the frozen memory on all four.
numbers: RegAgent SR / EHRAgent ACC / AgentDriver SR / CIC-IoT ACC. Fixed memory 67.53 / 16.75 / 40.11 / 71.50. Add-all 55.48 / 13.05 / 32.32 / 59.90. Coarse LLM judges C1 63.18 / 26.19 / 36.92 / 74.00; C3 (judge fine-tuned on 300 examples) 67.35 / 34.66 / 47.37 / 79.50. Strict 70.95 / 38.50 / 51.00 / 85.40.
limits: Strict evaluator is a simulated oracle using ground truth. Memory sizes differ (fixed 50-180, add-all up to 4100), so tokens are not matched. Column-to-agent mapping taken from the table header.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the value of Retain depends on the quality gate. Unfiltered write-back can cost 8 to 12 points. Gate writes on verified success.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: An Empirical Study of Experience-Following Behavior
finding: Experience-following: the more similar a retrieved case is to the query, the more the output copies it (near-perfect correlation). So wrong cases propagate. Deleting cases that proved useless later helps with a strict judge.
numbers: Error-propagation test: same retrieved inputs but ground-truth outputs gives an immediate gap, and add-all and coarse additions widen it over the run. With strict addition AgentDriver reaches the error-free variant after about 2000 executions. Deletion with strict judge kept or beat no deletion at far fewer records (RegAgent 70.95 at 2938 records vs 67.65 at 949; AgentDriver 51.00 at 1178 vs 49.97-51.81 at 323-846).
limits: Similarity correlation read from figures. Deletion gains vary a lot by judge quality.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: retrieved cases hurt when they are wrong and similar, since the model imitates them. Retrieval quality alone is not enough; case correctness matters. Prune cases by later-use utility.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: Test-Time Learning with Adaptive Memory
finding: On non-agentic reasoning tasks, curated memory beat plain retrieval of past input-output pairs (DR) in most cells, but not everywhere. Retrieval alone could also lower accuracy.
limits: AIME 2024 and 2025 have 30 questions each, so one question is 3.3 points. GPT-4o Game of 24 jump comes from storing a Python solver, so it is a tool-reuse effect. Claude Sonnet moved only 12 to 14 on Game of 24. Tokens not matched; DC adds a curator call.
agent_relevance: Closest to our non-agentic setting. Raw cases (DR) help on hard math but can hurt (GPT-4o Game of 24 DR 6 vs BL 10; MMLU-Pro Eng). Run a raw-vs-distilled arm and a no-memory arm.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: Test-Time Learning with Adaptive Memory
finding: Appending the full history (FH) of past turns did worse than curated memory and can fall below the baseline.
numbers: AIME 2024: Sonnet FH 26.7 vs DC methods 50.0 (baseline 23.3). GPT-4o FH 6.7 vs DC-RS 40.0 (baseline 20.0).
limits: 30 questions. Authors say FH also inflates context and cost. Only AIME 2024 in this table.
agent_relevance: Dumping all cases into context is a worse control than a small selected set; matched-token tests must cap raw cases.

source: Wei et al. (2025/2026) Evo-Memory: Benchmarking LLM Agent Test-time Learning with Self-Evolving Memory
finding: A broad benchmark (10 datasets, over 10 memory modules). A simple raw-experience retrieval baseline (ExpRAG) was strong and beat several more complex memory designs. Distilled or summarising memories (Mem0, A-Mem, DC, AWM) added little on single-turn reasoning.
numbers: Gemini-2.5 Flash single-turn: ReMem 0.65 average exact match (text). In one table panel, baseline-like rows (ReAct, Amem, Self-RAG, Mem0, DC-Cu, DC-RS, AWM) sit near 0.29 to 0.31 average while ExpRAG is 0.50 and ExpRecent 0.39. Multi-turn: ReMem/ExpRAG 0.92/0.96 on BabyAI.
limits: Table text was garbled in extraction; panel and column mapping is uncertain, so only the direction is firm. Authors propose ReMem and ExpRAG, so they are not neutral.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 contradicting DC: raw experience retrieval is a hard-to-beat baseline in this benchmark. Raw-vs-distilled is not predictable from task type alone yet.

source: Wei et al. (2025/2026) Evo-Memory: Benchmarking LLM Agent Test-time Learning with Self-Evolving Memory
finding: Memory gain tracks how similar tasks are inside a dataset. Storing both successes and failures without filtering hurt baseline memory methods; evolving methods stayed robust.
numbers: Correlation of ReMem gain over the history baseline with within-dataset task similarity: Pearson 0.717 (Gemini 2.5 Flash), 0.563 (Claude 3.7 Sonnet). PDDL and AlfWorld (tight clusters) gain most.
limits: Few datasets, so r rests on about 10 points. Similarity measured by embedding distance to cluster centre. Table 3 (failures) values not cleanly readable.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a similarity level matters. Cases help most where tasks recur in structure; with diverse tasks gain is small. Measure embedding similarity of our task set before relying on cases.

source: Zhang et al. (2025/2026) Agentic Context Engineering (ACE), ICLR 2026
finding: Distilled summaries lose detail (brevity bias) and rewriting a memory in full can collapse it. Adaptive memory also degrades without reliable feedback.
numbers: AppWorld case: context of 18,282 tokens (accuracy 66.7) collapsed in one step to 122 tokens (accuracy 57.1), below the 63.7 no-adaptation baseline. ACE vs Dynamic Cheatsheet on agent tasks: average +7.6 points; AppWorld average 59.4 (ACE) vs 51.9 (DC-Cu) vs 42.4 (ReAct).
limits: Authors built ACE, so a competing-method bias is likely. Single collapse case study. Without ground-truth labels both ACE and DC can degrade.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: summaries are not free; keep itemised, incremental, case-sized entries and not one rewritten summary. Gap 2: feedback quality gates all memory gains.

source: Agent KB: Leveraging Cross-Domain Experience for Agentic Problem Solving (2025, ICLR 2026)
finding: Adapting (refining) retrieved experiences beat replaying raw workflow logs; removing refine cost the most. Pass@2 adds failure diagnoses from the first attempt.
numbers: smolagents + GPT-4.1 on GAIA val (pass@1 avg): no KB 55.15; full 61.21; w/ raw workflow 58.18; w/o Refine 55.15; w/o Retrieve 57.58; w/o Reason 60.00. Full pass@3 reaches 73.9 (+18.7).
limits: GAIA val has 165 tasks, so one task is about 0.6 points. Authors' own system. Distilled experiences were reported on par with hand-curated ones.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the adapt step is what turns a case into gain, more than raw storage. Consistent with CLAVIER's reliance on user adaptation.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Memento's CBR gain is measured against the same planner and executor without CBR, so the offline-online contamination gap does not explain it. The -18.0 F1 is the offline-to-online executor step, not the CBR step.
numbers: CBR over Memento w/o CBR (F1 / PM): HLE +4.5 / +7.0 (22.2/17.4 to 26.7/24.4); SimpleQA +3.7 / +5.3; DeepResearcher +6.7 / +8.2 (59.9/72.2 to 66.6/80.4). Online executor 30.8/60.7 vs offline 48.8/62.8 on DeepResearcher.
limits: Still a single-team result with no seeds and no random-case control. The case bank is built from the training stream of the same task type, and a bank stocked with answers from the same benchmark could leak; GAIA val is used both to fill the bank and to score (test uses the bank from val: 87.88 val vs 79.40 test).
agent_relevance: Gap 8 mostly closed on the narrow point: the CBR delta is same-pipeline. A leak through the case bank is not excluded.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Memento stores both successful and failed trajectories with a reward, but has no success-only ablation. Most of the gain comes at K=1 retrieved case, and K up to 32 does not hurt.
limits: One dataset family, planner GPT-4.1, executor o4-mini. Cases are retrieved by a learned or similarity retriever (not random).
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open for Memento itself. K=1 does most of the work; that sets a floor for token-matched tests.

source: Guo et al. (2025) Re4 (KDD 2025), Retain ablation re-read
finding: Removing the Retain step (case bank frozen, RAG-like) made the system significantly worse online, because the product software and modules keep changing. Retained cases were human-revised test scripts.
numbers: About 6,000 recent online samples on two product units. CBR+Re4 beats deployed CBR+SFT by 2.75% (DCN) and 10.08% (SP) FF1. The w/o Retain curve is plotted far below, with annotations -78.65% and -69.22%.
limits: Size still not confirmed: the two negative values appear in the figure but I could not see whether they are the endpoint or the lowest point of the curve (no image renderer in this session). They are relative to CBR+SFT, not absolute FF1.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 only partly closed: direction is certain, size is large but exact value unverified. The Retain cases pass a human check, matching Xiong's finding that gated write-back is what pays.

source: Sourati et al. (2023) CBR with LMs for logical fallacies, re-read for case-base size
finding: The 10 percent case base best result comes from a grid of only four ratios (0.1, 0.4, 0.7, 1.0), no seeds or variance are reported, and the paper says two different things about size.
numbers: Abstract: size of the case database has negligible effect. Body: 10% gives the best performance and performance decreases continuously with higher percentages; one case (k=1) was also best. CBR beats vanilla LMs by 2.5-6 F1 in-domain and up to 8 out-of-domain.
limits: Fine-tuned small LMs (BERT, RoBERTa, ELECTRA), not prompted LLMs. Differences between neighbouring ratios are small and unreplicated.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: treat 10 percent best as a weak, unreplicated, possibly noise result. Do not generalise it to LLM agents. The consistent part is that k=1 is enough.

source: Hennessy and Hinkle (1992) Applying CBR to autoclave loading, IEEE Expert 7(5); Mark (1989) CLAVIER
finding: Not read. The IEEE page returned no text to the fetch tool and the search APIs were rate limited (429) or out of budget, so Mark 1989 and Hennessy and Hinkle 1992 stay unread.
limits: Paywalled. No full text available through the tools in this session.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open. Keep all CLAVIER numbers sourced to Hinkle and Toomey 1994 and 1995.

source: Search for a controlled before/after study of a 1990s deployed CBR system (gap 6)
finding: No controlled study with N and a baseline was found. The only quasi-baseline results in the sources already read are SMART (under 50% vs 87%, N not stated) and FormTool (64 of 100 colours cheaper). Search tools were rate limited, so the negative is weak.
limits: Absence of evidence from a limited search, not a proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Treat 1990s deployment numbers as builder reports; the modern controlled evidence is the LLM studies above.

source: Search for an LLM test of a context filter on case retrieval (gap 9)
finding: No paper found that tests a same-situation-different-environment filter for LLM case retrieval. Indirect evidence only: experience-following (d05) and similarity-gain correlation (d09).
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open. Our own test: tag cases with environment fields and compare filtered vs unfiltered retrieval, plus a random-case control.
